title: Event Emitter
statement:
Write a class `EventEmitter` that lets callbacks listen to named events and runs them when an event fires. It has two methods:

- `subscribe(eventName, callback)` registers `callback` as a listener of `eventName`. An event may have any number of listeners. It returns a subscription object with a method `unsubscribe()`, which removes that callback from the event's listeners and returns `undefined`.
- `emit(eventName, args)` calls every callback currently listening to `eventName`, in the order they subscribed, passing the items of the array `args` as separate arguments (`args` may be left out, which means no arguments). It returns an array of the callbacks' return values in that same order, or `[]` when the event has no listeners.

No two subscribed callbacks are the same function object.

Each case gives two lists of the same length, `actions` and `values`, run in order:

- `"EventEmitter"` (always first, `values[i]` is `[]`) creates the emitter and adds `[]` to the answer.
- `"subscribe"` with `[eventName, callback]` subscribes a new function built from the description `callback` and adds `["subscribed"]`. A description is one of:
  - `{ "returns": v }`: a function that ignores its arguments and returns `v`;
  - `{ "join": sep }`: a function that returns its arguments joined into one string with `sep` between them, like `(...args) => args.join(sep)`;
  - `{ "add": k }`: a function that returns `k` plus the sum of its arguments.
- `"emit"` with `[eventName]` or `[eventName, args]` adds `["emitted", results]`, where `results` is what `emit` returned.
- `"unsubscribe"` with `[k]` calls `unsubscribe()` on the object returned by the `k`-th `subscribe` action (counting from 0 over all subscribe actions) and adds `["unsubscribed", k]`. Each subscription is cancelled at most once.
constraints: actions[i] is "EventEmitter", "subscribe", "emit" or "unsubscribe"; only actions[0] is "EventEmitter"
"subscribe" takes an event name and a callback description
"emit" takes an event name and, optionally, an array of numbers to pass to the callbacks
"unsubscribe" takes the 0-based index of an earlier subscription that is still active
api: class EventEmitter { subscribe(eventName: string, callback: (...args: any[]) => any): { unsubscribe(): void }; emit(eventName: string, args?: any[]): any[] }
notes:
## Intuition

The emitter is a lookup table: from each event name to the callbacks listening to it, kept in subscription order. `subscribe` adds to the right bucket, `emit` runs that bucket. The interesting part is `unsubscribe`: it takes no arguments, so it must already know which bucket and which callback to remove. Returning an arrow function that closes over `listeners` and `callback` gives it exactly that. (The brute force keeps every subscription in one list with an `active` flag and scans the whole list on each `emit`; simple, but slower when there are many events.)

## Approach

1. Keep `events`, a `Map` from an event name to a `Set` of callbacks. A `Set` iterates in insertion order and deletes in O(1).
2. `subscribe`: create the event's `Set` the first time, add `callback` to it, and return `{ unsubscribe }`, whose function deletes `callback` from that same `listeners` set.
3. `emit`: look up `listeners`; with none, return `[]`. Otherwise call each callback with `...args` and return the results in order.

## Example 1, step by step

- `emit("firstEvent")` finds no listeners and returns `[]`.
- Two `subscribe` calls put the callbacks returning 5 and 6 (`{ "returns": 5 }` and `{ "returns": 6 }`) into the `firstEvent` set, in that order.
- `emit("firstEvent")` uses the default `args = []`, calls both callbacks and returns `[5, 6]`.

The answer is `[[], ["emitted", []], ["subscribed"], ["subscribed"], ["emitted", [5, 6]]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) for `subscribe` and `unsubscribe`; O(k) for `emit` with k listeners, plus their own work.
- Space: O(s) for s active subscriptions.

## Pitfalls

- `emit` must spread `args` into the callback: `callback(...args)`, not `callback(args)`, which hands over the whole array as one argument. In Example 4 the `add` callback would then compute `2 + [5]` and give the string `"25"` instead of 7.
- Forgetting the default for `args` makes `...args` throw when `emit` is called with just a name.
- Removing by position with a stored index breaks once an earlier callback has been removed; remove the callback itself.
- A plain object keyed by event name trips over names such as `"constructor"`; a `Map` has no such keys.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `events` | map from an event name to the set of its callbacks |
| `listeners` | the callback set of one event |
| `callback` | a subscribed function |
| `args` | arguments passed to every callback of an `emit` |
